newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia landslide rescuers race against weather.
newsitem.headline: Australia landslide rescuers race against weather.

text.p: Rescuers on Monday raced against the weather to find eight people still buried in the rubble of a landslide at an Australian ski resort, urged on by prayers for another miracle survivor.

Rescuers worked frantically to shield the dangerously unstable debris from approaching rain, but some good news surfaced on Monday when a woman assumed to have been trapped in the debris turned up alive and well.
The woman was thought to have been swept off her feet by the landslide late on Wednesday night, burying her along with the 19 occupants of two ski lodges destroyed in the disaster.

But she was never in danger, police told Reuters. She and her husband were staying in a nearby lodge when the landslide hit and they rushed to the scene to help mount a rescue. They became separated and her husband reported her missing.
They found each other and left the Thredbo resort, southwest of Sydney, but rescuers listed the woman as missing until Monday when she came forward. Police declined to identify her.
"We originally thought there was 20 people involved. There are only 19 people involved," State Coroner Derek Hand said.
Working under helium-filled lanterns on Monday night, rescuers began erecting big sheets of plastic over the five-day-old heap of concrete slabs, twisted metal and dirt.
If left uncovered, rain could send the debris crashing further down the steep hillside and flood the honeycomb of tunnels rescuers have dug in search of the missing, police said.
"We are very concerned about the weather," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters.
Rain and snow was originally forecast for Thredbo on Thursday, but could now come on Tuesday, he said.

It has been two nights since ski instructor Stuart Diver, 27, emerged from the rubble alive after 64 hours entombed in a concrete sarcophagus, but about 500 people gathered at Thredbo's small sun-lit church on Monday afternoon to pray for another miracle.
Ten bodies have been recovered and eight are still missing.
"We can only hope and pray that we find more people alive," ambulance superintendent Allan Dent said after the service.

The chances of finding more survivors were diminishing with every night of sub-zero temperatures. The rescue effort is further frustrated by shifting boulders and dirt, forcing crews to temporarily leave the site for fear of another collapse.
"We pray in grief for lives lost and those which may hang in the balance. For those who sorrow and those who search," Anglican Reverend Harvey Sloane told the tearful congregation.
Grieving family and friends of those missing, rescuers and politicians also gave thanks for Diver's survival.
"He (Diver) wants everyone to know that he can move his toes even better than before. His spirits are good," said acting prime minister Tim Fischer.
Fischer had visited Diver in a hospital in nearby Canberra, where he was making a speedy recovery. Doctors had feared Diver might need surgery to treat severe frostbite to his feet.
Outside the church, villagers linked arms, hugged and wept. Ski instructors and ski rescue staff, who had hurried down from the snowfields for the service, were overcome with emotion.
Rescuers have honeycombed the landslide debris with 24 metres (80 feet) of tunnels, burrowing by hand if need be to look for cavities that might hide life.
Diver's wife, Sally, was also buried in the landslide. They were in bed together when the disaster struck.
Diver has told rescuers how he pressed his nose against a concrete slab above his head in order to breathe as water and mud filled his concrete tomb.
Some rescuers have said Diver tried desperately to save his wife after the landslide hit, but her fate is still unclear.
